summary: You’ll learn how to sell combo meals on the phone with clear scripts, pricing checks, and upsell steps that fit real restaurant calls.
intro:
Restaurant combo meals sell best on the phone when they are easy to hear, easy to repeat, and easy to price. The trick is not to talk more. It is to say the combo name, what comes with it, and the total in a simple order.

For a pizza shop, deli, or family restaurant, the phone is often where combo sales are won or lost. A caller who is already hungry does not want a long menu. They want a clear deal, a quick yes or no on swaps, and a ready time they can trust.

sections.h2: What should I say when someone asks about combo meals?
sections.body:
Start with the combo name first, then the important parts. Do not read the whole menu. Keep the sentence short so the caller can decide fast.

A good phone line sounds like this: “Our chicken parm combo is $18.95 and comes with salad and garlic bread. Would you like the regular or the spicy version?” That gives the price, the included sides, and one easy choice.

Use this quick structure for every combo:
1. Name the deal.
2. Say the price.
3. Say what is included.
4. Ask one question only.

| Combo part | Example |
|---|---|
| Item name | Chicken parm combo |
| Price | $18.95 |
| Included | Salad and garlic bread |
| Choice | Regular or spicy |

If your menu has several combo meals, keep the names short and different from each other. “Lunch special,” “family special,” and “pizza special” are easier to hear than three similar names with long details. ROAL reads the live menu, so if the combo is listed clearly there, the phone host can answer the question the same way each time.

sections.h2: How do I keep combo orders from turning into long back-and-forth calls?
sections.body:
Most long calls happen because the menu is not organized for ordering. The best fix is to make the combo easy to say and easy to modify. That means fewer words, fewer choices, and fewer hidden details.

Use a simple order flow like this:
1. Caller asks for the combo.
2. You confirm the base item.
3. You ask for one modifier group at a time, like side, drink, or protein.
4. You repeat the full order back.
5. You give the ready time.

Example script: “Just to confirm, you want the turkey club combo with fries and a Coke, correct?” Then: “That comes to $15.50, and it’ll be ready in about 20 minutes.”

A useful checklist for combo calls:
- Do I know the exact combo name?
- Did I state the total before taking extras?
- Did I ask about one upgrade at a time?
- Did I repeat the full order back?

This matters because callers often order faster by phone than in person. If the combo is easy to hear, the order moves quicker and your staff spends less time clarifying the same details.

sections.h2: How should I price combo meals so they still make sense on the phone?
sections.body:
Phone callers need the price stated plainly. If you hide the combo price inside a long explanation, they may compare it to delivery apps or just hang up. Say the deal value clearly, then move on.

Here is a simple way to think about it. Say your burger combo is $14.99 and your burger alone is $11.99. The combo adds fries and a drink for $3 more. That is easy to explain on the phone and easy for the caller to compare.

Use this swap-in example for your own menu:
- Burger alone: your price
- Fries: your price
- Drink: your price
- Combo price: the bundled price

If you want to see the effect on phone orders, compare one order two ways:
- Individual items: burger + fries + drink
- Combo: bundled meal with a clear price

The point is not to force every caller into a combo. It is to make the deal obvious when it fits their order. That works especially well for lunch specials, family meals, and late-night takeout. For more menu structure ideas, see [making your menu easy to order by phone](/blog/restaurant-menu-for-phone-orders) and [lunch specials that drive takeout calls](/blog/lunch-specials-takeout).

sections.h2: What upsell questions work without sounding pushy?
sections.body:
The best upsell is one that helps the caller finish the meal, not one that sounds like a sales pitch. Ask about one add-on after the main combo is set.

Good examples:
- “Would you like to make that a large for $2 more?”
- “Would you like to add a soup or salad to that combo?”
- “Do you want any extra dressing or sauce on the side?”

Bad examples are long and vague, like asking three upsells at once. That slows the order and can make the caller second-guess the whole meal.

A practical upsell order for combo meals:
1. Main combo.
2. Size upgrade.
3. Side or drink add-on.
4. Sauce, seasoning, or extra item.

Worked example: say your average combo is $17 and a large upgrade is $2.50. If one out of every four callers says yes, that upgrade adds $0.62 on average per combo order. Plug in your own numbers to see what matters for your menu. The idea is simple: one clean upsell question can improve the ticket without making the caller feel pressured.

ROAL can ask order questions in the caller’s language, confirm the order back, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen, which helps keep these upsells accurate.

sections.h2: How do I handle sold-out items and special requests on combo orders?
sections.body:
Combo meals get messy when one piece is unavailable. If a combo includes a sold-out item, the phone host should not offer it. The caller should hear a clear replacement option instead of a promise the kitchen cannot fill.

Use a script like this: “The chicken combo is unavailable right now, but I can offer the turkey combo or the tuna combo instead.” That is faster than apologizing and re-reading the whole menu.

For special requests, keep the answer short and practical:
- Swaps: yes or no based on your kitchen rules
- Allergies: hand off to staff with a summary
- Complaints: hand off to staff with a summary
- Manager requests: hand off to staff with a summary

Short checklist for tricky combo calls:
- Is the item sold out?
- Is the swap allowed?
- Did I note the special request clearly?
- Does staff need to handle this directly?

If your restaurant has lunch, dinner, and catering menus, keep the combo names separate so the caller does not mix them up. ROAL can read menu data from your website, menu PDFs, menu photos, or an upload, which makes it easier to keep combo items current when the menu changes.

sections.h2: What should I track to know if combo meals are working on the phone?
sections.body:
Do not track everything. Track the few numbers that tell you whether combo ordering is helping or hurting.

Use this simple owner checklist each week:
- Which combo is asked for most often?
- Which combo causes the most questions?
- Which add-on gets accepted most often?
- Which item gets sold out too early?
- Which call script leads to the fewest corrections?

A simple table can help:

| Combo | Calls per week | Common question | Fix |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Burger combo | plug in your number | Size upgrade? | Add a clear large-upgrade line |
| Pasta combo | plug in your number | Side choice? | List the side before the caller asks |
| Family meal | plug in your number | Feeds how many? | Put the serving count in the name |

If you use ROAL, you can review call history with transcripts and recordings, plus menu editor and upsell suggestions in the dashboard. That makes it easier to spot where callers hesitate and where your combo wording needs a cleanup.

A lot of owners find that the menu itself is the problem, not the caller. If the combo is easy to say, easy to hear, and easy to repeat, phone orders feel smoother for everyone. If you want to try that setup, [build a free test host from your website](/try).

sections.h2: FAQ: common owner questions about combo meals on the phone
sections.body:
**Should I list combo meals first when answering the phone?**
Yes, if combo meals are one of your main sellers. Say the combo name early and keep the price close to it. That helps callers decide fast without hearing the full menu.

**Can I offer combo swaps by phone?**
Yes, but only the swaps your kitchen can actually handle. Keep the swap rules simple and consistent so the order does not get messy at the prep table.

**What if the caller wants a combo and a few extra items?**
Take the combo first, then add extras one by one. Repeat the full order back before you quote the ready time. That keeps the ticket clean.

**Does ROAL take card payments over the phone?**
No. It takes items, modifiers, notes, name, and phone number, then sends the order to the kitchen screen. Payment happens at pickup or however your restaurant already takes it.

takeaways: Say the combo name, price, and included items in one short line.
Ask one upsell question at a time so the call stays fast.
Keep sold-out combo items off the phone menu.
Use a clean script and repeat the full order back before the ready time.

faq.q: How do I sell combo meals on the phone without sounding pushy?
faq.a: Keep it short and specific. Say the combo name, the price, and what comes with it, then ask one simple follow-up question. That sounds helpful, not pushy, and it keeps the call moving.

faq.q: What should I say when a caller wants a combo meal with changes?
faq.a: Confirm the base combo first, then handle one change at a time. For example: “Do you want fries or a salad with that?” After you collect the changes, repeat the full order back so the caller can confirm it.

faq.q: How can I make phone combo orders faster for my staff?
faq.a: Use shorter combo names, fewer choices, and a clear order script. If the menu is easy to read and the ticket is clean, staff spends less time clarifying details. ROAL can help by reading the live menu and sending a clean ticket to the kitchen screen.

faq.q: Should I change my combo prices for phone orders?
faq.a: Not unless your restaurant already uses different pricing by channel. Most owners do better when the phone price is simple and consistent. If you want to compare pricing models, look at your actual ticket size and the time your staff spends on each call.
